AlternateTargets: originally there is not a single thing
from the first, not one thing
Senses.Explanation: (本來) from the root / origin, originally + (無) there is no + (一物) one thing: "from the origin, not one thing." The line is the third of (慧能)'s verse in the received (宗寶) (六祖大師法寶壇經): (菩提本無樹)，(明鏡亦非臺)；(本來無一物)，(何處惹塵埃) (the text writes his name 惠能). The corpus shows the line is a feature of the LATER Platform-Sutra text: the Dunhuang (壇經) (T48n2007) gives the same verse with the third line "the buddha-nature is ever pure" (佛性常清淨，何處有塵埃), without (本來無一物). Across the lamp records the couplet varies — (何處惹塵埃) (法寶壇經); (何處有塵埃) (祖堂集, which carries the verse twice, with first lines 菩提本無樹 and 身非菩提樹); and (本來無一物何假拂塵埃) with first line (菩提本非樹) (傳燈玉英集). Zen-scoped the phrase occurs 214 hits / 106 texts; the contracted (本無一物) 34 / 30. Attested deployment beyond the verse: (洞山良价) issues a verdict on the line — asked why (神秀)'s (時時勤拂拭) verse did not win the robe, (洞山答曰)：「(直道本來無一物)，(也未得衣缽在)。」 (祖堂集), and (師有時垂語曰直道本來無一物猶未消得佗鉢袋子) (傳燈玉英集): even to say "from the origin, not one thing" has not yet earned the robe-and-bowl. (黃檗希運) in the (宛陵錄) quotes (本來無一物何處有塵埃), and when a monk asks "from the origin not one thing — is 'no-thing' then it?" (本來無一物無物便是否) answers "even 'no-thing' is not it" (無亦不是). The line is also raised as a stock tag, e.g. (舉六祖云本來無一物長慶云萬象之中獨露身). The texts assign the phrase no gloss beyond its literal sense, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. Primary attribution: (慧能)'s verse in the received (六祖大師法寶壇經) (T48n2008, 行由第一; the text spells the name 惠能, roster 慧能, editor 宗寶). The (傳燈玉英集) verse-variant (本非樹…何假拂塵埃) is the SAME Platform-Sutra episode transmitted in a Jingde-lamp digest, so attributed to (慧能) with the variant noted. (洞山良价) is the named speaker of the verdict (洞山答曰… / 師[=洞山]有時垂語…) in (祖堂集) and (傳燈玉英集) — two independent witnesses. (黃檗希運) in the (宛陵錄) (inside 古尊宿語錄, cb:mulu 黃檗斷際禪師宛陵錄); he quotes the couplet twice (0633b04, 0636c03). The B27n0152 raising (paired with 長慶's line) is a later stock raising, so MasterName null. The Dunhuang (佛性常清淨) reading is reported for contrast only and is NOT an occurrence of this headword — T48n2007 is therefore deliberately not listed in SourceTexts. Multi-source: (壇經), (祖堂集), (傳燈玉英集), (古尊宿語錄); masters (慧能), (洞山良价), (黃檗希運).

Occurrences.Kwic: 問本來無一物無物便是否師云無亦不是菩提無是處

Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄), (小叅); a raised stock tag — (舉六祖云本來無一物長慶云萬象之中獨露身). A later raising pairing (慧能)'s line with (長慶)'s, so MasterName null per the raised-case rule.

AlternateTargets: the face you had before your parents were born
Senses.Explanation: Literally 'the face one originally has.' Its origin is the Dayu Ridge story: the monk Huiming, chasing Huineng for the robe, cannot lift it; Huineng says 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — right at such a moment, which is Elder Ming's original face?' (不思善，不思惡，正恁麼時，阿那箇是明上座本來面目), and Ming is awakened. From this it becomes one of the corpus's most common test-questions, above all in the form 'your original face before your father and mother were born' (父母未生前本來面目). In the record the answer is characteristically shown rather than defined: Fuchuan (覆船) sticks out his tongue; a Dongshan-line master answers 'not walking the bird's path' (不行鳥道) and 'seeing mountains as mountains, seeing waters as waters' (見山是山，見水是水). Asked head-on, 'what is … the original face?' (如何是…本來面目) is a standing test-question (274 hits in 116 allowlist texts); recorded exchanges include 'What is your original face?' — 'Eyebrows horizontal, nose straight' (「如何是你本來面目？」師云：「眉橫鼻直。」, J28nB210), and the monk who says 'it cannot be known by wisdom, cannot be cognized by consciousness' and is told 'I asked about your original face and you give me all these principles' (僧云：「不可以智知，不可以識識。」師云：「問汝本來面目，說許多道理」, J28nB202); in J28nB209 the monk's 'the wind cannot blow it away' (風刮不著) is met with 'Say more!' (師云：「更道看！」) — the monk is speechless, and the master strikes (僧無語，師便棒). The corpus's own lists of what students investigate name it among the standard sayings: 'some investigate the word no (無); some investigate the original face; some investigate who-is-reciting-the-buddha's-name — the cases differ, the doubt investigated is the same' (或有參無字者。或有參本來面目者。或有參究念佛者。公案雖異疑究是同, T48n2021; likewise J38nB429 'such as those investigating the original face before father and mother were born, or investigating who is the one reciting the buddha's name' 如參父母未生前本來面目者，或參念佛底是誰者, and J28nB208). On the origin story itself, one record cites 'which one is your original face, elder?' (阿那個是你上座本來面目) and asks: 'when did he ever say that the moment of not thinking good or evil IS your original face?' (亦何曾說不思善惡時，即是你本來面目乎？, J25nB174).
Senses.Note: Overwhelmingly attested (1320 hits across 264 allowlist texts) and uniform — no master bends the base meaning, so a single corpus-wide sense is honest. Some later masters (the line of Nanyue Jiqi 南嶽繼起 and Sanfeng Hanyue 三峰漢月, J34nB301) 'forbid even mentioning the original face' (不許人提著本來面目). Collocations (allowlist grep): the explicit question-form 'the original face before father and mother were born' (父母未生前本來面目) 92 hits in 57 texts (the framing 'before father and mother were born, which is your original face?' 父母未生已前，那箇是你本來面目 also attested, J28nB208); the pointing formula 'this is your original face' (是汝／你本來面目) 70 hits in 44 texts (plus the same phrase with the variant graph for 'your', 是爾本來面目, twice).

Occurrences.Kwic: 盧曰：不思善，不思惡，正恁麼時，阿那箇是明上座本來面目？師當下大悟，徧體汗流，泣禮數拜
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Dayu Ridge origin story (Huineng to Huiming), here in the Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書). The locus classicus of the phrase: 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — which is Elder Ming's original face?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問：「如何是父母未生前本來面目？」門云：「今日汝且隨我往頂山寺，回來與汝說。」門回，師跪而啟曰：「如今求老和尚為某甲說。」門驀豎起拳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The dominant question-form 'the original face before your parents were born' (父母未生前本來面目), put to the master as the saying under investigation; the master's answer is a suddenly raised fist (驀豎起拳). Independent witness in a Jiaxing-canon recorded-sayings collection (語錄).

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「三峰老和尚不許人提著本來面目，和尚尋常不許人提著本來面目，因什今日又要這上座明取本來面目？」師曰：「哀哉！法門不幸。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Sanfeng / Nanyue Jiqi line forbids even mentioning the original face (不許人提著本來面目) — the monk presses the master on the inconsistency; the master answers 'Alas! Misfortune for the teaching gate' (哀哉！法門不幸).

AlternateTargets: the matter of one's own lot
Senses.Explanation: The graphs join 'one's own portion, allotment, or lot' (本分) to 'matter or affair' (事): the matter that belongs to one's own basic lot. The corpus sets it against 'outside one's lot' or 'extra' (分外) and records about 840 occurrences across 184 allowlisted texts. It is repeatedly asked as 'what is one's own fundamental matter?' (如何是本分事), 'what is the student's own fundamental matter?' (如何是學人本分事), and 'what is a monk's own fundamental matter?' (如何是衲僧本分事). In the early Patriarchs' Hall Collection (祖堂集), an official tells an old monk, 'one who has left home has an own-lot matter; what is your own-lot matter, monk?' (出家自有本分事。作摩生是和尚本分事？), and the monk has no reply (無對). A later record directly defines it: 'the own-lot matter is where the person's own root-destiny comes to rest' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). Asked 'what is Shanglan's own-lot matter?' (如何是上藍本分事), Shanglan answers, 'not borrowed from the thousand sages, not sought among the myriad devices' (不從千聖借豈向萬機求). Zhaozhou says a lineage master must 'receive people with the own-lot matter' (以本分事接人). Another master points at the questioner and says, 'it is your own matter' (是你本分事); another says, 'eating gruel and rice is your own matter' (喫粥喫飯是汝本分事). A recorded contrast says, 'the moment you speak of the own-lot matter, it has already become extra' (你纔說本分事早是分外了). The same 'own-lot' graph family includes 'own-lot fodder' (本分草料), 'own-lot tongs and hammer' (本分鉗鎚), and 'an own-lot master of the lineage' (本分宗師).
Senses.Note: This is the Chan technical use, not the ordinary role-duty sense recorded separately below. The corpus itself glosses it as "the own-lot matter is where the person's own root-destiny comes to rest" (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). Grep-verified counts (Zen allowlist): bare (本分) 2,482 hits in 321 texts; (本分事) as a contiguous string 773 in 181 (line-split hits raise the raw total toward the ~840 above).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰不從千聖借豈向萬機求
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (Wang Sui's abridgement of the Jingde-era transmission record); answer of (洪州上藍令超禪師) (Chan master Lingchao of Shanglan, Hongzhou) to the stock question on the prior line (如何是上藍本分事, 'what is Shanglan's own-lot matter?'). The answer states the own-lot matter is not borrowed from the sages nor sought among the myriad devices.

AlternateTargets: the business proper to one's role
Senses.Explanation: In ordinary institutional use, 'one's proper duty' (本分事) is the business that belongs to a person's role. A monastic admonition calls keeping the precepts a bhikshu's proper duty, then condemns neglect of rules and disorderly conduct. This is an assigned role-duty, not the fundamental matter asked about in Chan public exchanges.
Senses.Note: One allowlisted source presently anchors this distinct ordinary use; it is kept separate because the referent is an assigned monastic duty rather than the Chan fundamental matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既稱比丘持戒是本分事，忽略繩趨，放蕩規矩，取玷法門，自招罪過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monastic admonition identifies keeping precepts as a bhikshu's proper duty and rebukes neglect of regulated conduct.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the primary or original investigation. The possessives and verbal predicates in later Chinese Chan records make its local use concrete. A hall leader is told to know each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; another passage says that not knowing a person's primary investigation leaves the leader without a way to act. Speakers tell people to place the saying under their primary investigation before their eyes, raise their primary investigation, or warn that they have dropped one line of it behind their head. The compound can take 'public case' or 'word, saying, conversational thread' after it, and can itself be said to be broken through. One direct question asks, 'What is primary investigation?' The answer gives a particular example: if one trusts the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate who is recollecting buddha; this is what that speaker calls primary investigation. Another text says that the Chan house relies on primary investigation and that when primary investigation breaks through it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. These predicates describe the assigned subject and the act of investigating it without turning the term into a named system.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 232 matches in 100 files. The expanded phrase 'word or saying under primary investigation' has eighty-nine matches in fifty files; 'raise the primary investigation' has twenty matches in fifteen; 'public case of primary investigation' has four in four; and 'one line of primary investigation' has three in three. One text has the only direct 'what is primary investigation?' formula and its own example; two texts use 'the so-called primary investigation.' The phrase is strongly possessive: texts say 'each person's,' 'one's own,' 'the one assigned,' and 'not knowing his.' No evidence supports treating it as an untranslated foreign object or as a master-specific sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何謂本參？若於念佛法門信得及，但參是誰念佛，所謂本參也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A reply to a layman asks, 'What is primary investigation?' It answers, 'If you trust the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate only who is recollecting buddha; this is what is called primary investigation.' This is the speaker's particular example, not the only saying attached to the compound elsewhere.

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲至堂中，先須識禪眾之號與貌，與各各本參話頭，然後可以垂手鍛鍊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A text on managing the hall says, 'Before going into the hall, first know the names and appearances of the Chan assembly and each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; only then can you extend a hand and apply the forge.'

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher tells each person, 'Place the word or saying under your primary investigation before you, as if leaning against Mount Sumeru. Let mind after mind have no interval and thought after thought no gap; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are also like this.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 你平日疑情不切，將一句本參丟在腦後，如今豎起脊梁，把話頭放在面前
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'Ordinarily your condition of doubt is not urgent; you throw one line of your primary investigation behind your head. Now straighten your spine and put the word or saying before you.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 提起本參，晝夜切磋，琢磨千生業障，一刻冰消瓦解
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'Raise the primary investigation; cut and polish it day and night. Grind away the obstructions of a thousand lives, and in one instant ice melts and tiles dissolve.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 宗中之相，惟據本參。本參破如月印千江
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A text says, 'The Chan house's form relies only on primary investigation. When primary investigation breaks through, it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本參公案急要翻身，胸次疑團直須打破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teacher says, 'At the public case of primary investigation, urgently turn over; the mass of doubt in your breast must be broken open.'

Senses.Explanation: Literally, native ground. The term occurs 529 times in 195 allowlisted texts. Its dominant Zen-loaded deployment is the fixed phrase 'native-ground scenery': records say to recognize one's original face and tread one's native-ground scenery, warn that wrong roads conceal each person's native-ground scenery, and ask that it be illuminated or fully seen through. A preface says the records return to the person's own native-ground scenery; teaching-seat records place it in bowing, turning, daily activity, or the lifting of a staff. The corpus treats this ground and its scenery as something belonging to each person and subject to public demand and display. It does not define it as a metaphysical substrate.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded referent. Split from the ordinary adjective 'local/native' because a person's figurative ground and local officials are different things.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse directly pairs recognizing the original face with treading native-ground scenery.

Senses.Explanation: As an ordinary adjective, the same graphs mean local or native to a place. The monastic code's imperial proclamation lists 'local officials' among military officers, envoys, common people, and monks. This administrative referent is different from a person's native ground and therefore receives its own sense.
Senses.Note: One clear curated Zen-allowlist witness currently anchors the ordinary administrative sense; it is kept separate under the different-thing test.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the native scenery of one's own ground
AlternateTargets: the scenery of one's home ground
Senses.Explanation: One's own ground or native place (本地), plus scenery or view (風光): Literally "the scenery of one's home ground." 382 occurrences across 161 allowlist files. The corpus pairs it with "original face" (本來面目): the two run together as "the native scenery of one's own ground, the original face" (本地風光本來面目; 4× in 2 files — Yuanwu's recorded sayings 圓悟語錄: 於動靜語默覺夢之間。無不皆是本地風光本來面目, "amid motion and stillness, speech and silence, waking and dream, there is nothing that is not the native scenery of one's own ground, the original face"; Dahui's recorded sayings 大慧語錄: 各人本地風光本來面目, "each person's own native scenery, original face") and stand in parallel clauses in Yuanwu Keqin's instructions: "step onto the native scenery of your own ground; clearly see the original face" (蹋著本地風光，明見本來面目) and "clearly attest the native scenery of your own ground; clearly see the original face" (明證本地風光，明見本來面目; both X69n1357). Attested verb collocations (allowlist, grep-verified): 'step onto the native scenery' (蹋著本地風光, 23× in 13 files), "clearly see," (明見本地風光 2×), "recognize for oneself," (自識本地風光 1× — Dahui: 故設方便誘引之。令其自識本地風光, "expedients are set up to lead one to recognize one's own native scenery"), "clearly attest," (明證本地風光 1×). Yuanwu's small-assembly talk sets it beside two negations: "treading on the native scenery of one's own ground — not following sound-and-form, not dwelling in profane or sacred" (踏著本地風光。不隨聲色不居凡聖). It is posed as a test question — "what is the native scenery of one's own ground?" (如何是本地風光; 8 allowlist files) — with recorded answers: "it has always been going in and out at your face-gate," (嘗在汝面門出入 Miyun's recorded sayings 密雲禪師語錄, J10nA158), "the heavens open, day after day new," (天開日日新 J27nB193), "the bright sun shines in mid-sky," (杲日麗中天 J37nB388), and raising the whisk with "do you see?" (見麼, J38nB424). One exchange draws a contrast with ordinary "scenery" (風光): asked "what is the native scenery of one's own ground?" (如何是本地風光), a layman answers "the crescent moon curves, shining on how many isles — how many people rejoice, how many grieve" (月子彎彎照幾洲，幾人歡樂幾人愁), and the questioner returns "I am not asking about that scenery," (不問者箇風光 X82n1571). The texts deploy the term through these pairings, verbs, and answers without assigning it a gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense recorded: the verb collocations and the pairing with "original face" (本來面目) recur across masters and centuries (counts in the explanation); no master-specific bending found. Extremely well attested (382 hits across 161 allowlist files). Keep the rendering on the graphs — "one's own ground," (本地) "scenery" (風光) — concrete; the texts do not state an abstraction ("the Absolute") in its place.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蹋著本地風光，明見本來面目
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Essentials of Mind of Chan Master Foguo Keqin (佛果克勤禪師心要 — Yuanwu Keqin's letters/instructions); governing head "shown to the monk Min" (示民上人) — his own "teaching words" (法語). The paired clauses "native scenery of one's own ground" (本地風光) / "original face" (本來面目), verb "step onto" (蹋著).

Occurrences.Kwic: 踏著本地風光。不隨聲色不居凡聖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo (圓悟佛果禪師語錄), head "small assembly 4" (小參四) — Yuanwu's small-assembly talk. Sets "treading on the native scenery of one's own ground" (踏著本地風光) beside "not following sound-and-form, not dwelling in profane or sacred" (不隨聲色不居凡聖).

Occurrences.Kwic: 故設方便誘引之。令其自識本地風光
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄), head "shown to the layman Miaoming, Li Bohe of the Secretariat" (示妙明居士李知省伯和) — Dahui's "teaching words" (法語) to a layman. Expedients are set up (故設方便誘引之, "therefore expedients are devised to lead him on") to lead one to recognize one's own native scenery (本地風光).

Occurrences.Kwic: 比丘尼問：「如何是本地風光？」師云：「嘗在汝面門出入。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun (密雲禪師語錄). A nun asks and the master answers, so MasterName is null under the two-speaker rule. The answerer is Miyun Yuanwu: 'it has always been going in and out at your face-gate' (嘗在汝面門出入).

Senses.Explanation: Original or root mind. The word occurs 748 times in 157 allowlisted texts. The Mirror Record says mind has no form, color, root, lodging, arising, extinction, or observable contemplation; if something observable can be carried out, that text assigns it to reception, conception, activity, and discrimination rather than original mind. The Platform Record pairs recognizing one’s original mind with seeing one’s original nature (若識自本心，見自本性). Other records say it is neither joined nor separate, reject the claim that it first needs stillness, and place original nature and original mind together. These are differing corpus predicates of one textual term, not a menu of interpretations.
Senses.Note: Primary inherited Buddhist/Chan sense. Cross-check original nature (本性), true mind, and no-mind as neighboring entries with their own predicates. No single imported metaphysical definition is imposed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心無形色。無根無住。無生無滅。亦無覺觀可行。若有可觀行者。即是受想行識。非是本心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says, 'Mind has no form or color, no root and no lodging, no arising and no extinction, nor any noticing or contemplating that can be carried out. If something observable can be carried out, it is reception, conception, activity, and discrimination; it is not original mind.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 欲識汝本心非合亦非離
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says, 'If you wish to recognize your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不識本心，學法無益；若識自本心，見自本性
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'Not recognizing original mind, studying the teaching is of no benefit; if you recognize your own original mind, see your own original nature.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本心不寂要假寂靜。本來寂故何用寂靜。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record rejects the claim that original mind is not still and therefore requires stillness: 'Because it is originally still, what use is stillness?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖祖佛佛只說如人。本性本心別無道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record says, 'The patriarchs and buddhas only speak according to the person: original nature and original mind, with no other principle.'

Senses.Explanation: A person’s prior intention or purpose. In one event account the speaker says, “this day’s affair was not my original intention” (此日之事，故非本心) and immediately explains that he had not intended even to reside on a mountain. In a succession discussion another speaker says that nobody had accorded with his original intention except Mingyuan (無有契我本心者). These event and decision contexts refer to intention, not original mind.
Senses.Note: Ordinary intention sense. Copies of the same “this day’s affair” event in several compilations were treated as one transmitted witness. The phrase “depart from original mind/intention” was excluded because its referent is ambiguous.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大眾，此日之事，故非本心。實謂祇箇住山寧有意，向來成佛亦無心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker says that the day’s event was not his original intention and immediately denies having intended even to reside on a mountain or become a buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我雖則繼席六載，無有契我本心者，惟明元隨我十餘年
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a succession discussion, the speaker says that during six years in the seat nobody accorded with his original intention except Mingyuan, who had followed him for more than ten years.

Senses.Explanation: One's nature as it is from the outset. Chan records repeatedly use 'see one's own original nature' beside 'recognize one's own original mind.' The Platform Record makes seeing it the distinction between remaining outside the gate and entering, and describes it as not arising or extinguishing. The Mirror Record says that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct. These are the texts' recorded descriptions; the English should preserve the plain noun phrase rather than substitute a later explanatory system. The omitted collocation "original nature empty" (本性空) occurs forty times in thirty texts, but it has more than one syntax. Twenty-seven occurrences in twenty-five texts belong to the fixed line, "understand body and mind, original nature empty; how would this person differ from buddha?" (了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別). A later Chan address raises that line and immediately comments, "the buddha-body is neither real nor empty; buddha-as-appearance is not appearance" (佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻). The Source-Mirror Record gives a separate explicit definition: "as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean" (本性空者，即是自性清淨心；本性即自性；空，即清淨義).
Senses.Note: The corpus has 667 matches in 152 files. The compound occurs in direct corrections, statements linking it with original mind, and descriptions of it as without difference. Six matches in six files explicitly pair original nature and original mind. The evidence supports one corpus-wide sense. The forty "original nature empty" matches are therefore not treated as forty copies of one bare equation. The fixed body-and-mind verse, the Source-Mirror definition, and the critical construction "rely on original-nature empty" (恃本性空, two occurrences in two texts) are distinct deployments. One Source-Mirror list criticizes people who follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty, alongside people who cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing (或隨結使而恃本性空，或執纏蓋而妄加除斷). Each predicate is reported as that text's wording rather than generalized beyond its occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝作此偈，未見本性，只到門外，未入門內。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'You composed this verse but have not seen original nature; you have only reached outside the gate and have not entered inside it.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 須得言下識自本心，見自本性不生不滅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'You must, at the words, recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, which does not arise and does not extinguish.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 若識自本心，見自本性，即名丈夫、天人師、佛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record says, 'If you recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, you are then named a great person, a teacher of humans and gods, a buddha.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 始知本性無差。非因行得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Mirror Record says, 'Only then is it known that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 本性本心別無道理。會取會取。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record says, 'Original nature and original mind: there is no other principle. Understand it; understand it.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋曰。本性空者。即是自性清淨心。本性即自性。空。即清淨義。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Source-Mirror Record explicitly says: as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或隨結使而恃本性空。或執纏蓋而妄加除斷。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Critical list: some follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty; others cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：拘留孫佛云：見身無實是佛身，了心如幻是佛幻，了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別？師云：佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan address raises the fixed verse: see the body as unreal, understand mind as appearance, understand body and mind as original-nature empty; it then comments that the buddha-body is neither real nor empty and buddha-as-appearance is not appearance.

AlternateTargets: originally there is not a single thing
Senses.Explanation: Literally, fundamentally or originally (本) there is not (無) one thing (一物): "fundamentally, not one thing." It occurs 34 times in 30 allowlisted texts. The close form "originally, not one thing" (本來無一物) occurs 214 times in 106 and is fixed in Huineng's verse: "the bodhi tree fundamentally has no tree; the bright mirror also is no stand; originally, not one thing; where could dust be attracted?" (菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺，本來無一物，何處惹塵埃). The exact shorter headword is deployed as a predicate and repeatedly challenged. The Collection of the Patriarchal Hall says that turning the light back to one's own mind-source and finding "fundamentally, not one thing" is called becoming buddha there, contrasting it with gradual certification through myriad deeds. Yinyuan versifies, "the scenery beyond is not heard in the world; fundamentally, not one thing to present to you" (那畔風光世莫聞，本無一物可呈君). Another passage holds together "three heads, six arms, a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, yet fundamentally not one thing" with "the myriad forms run crosswise." Most decisively, a student asks, "fundamentally, not one thing—what does the student investigate?" and the master answers, "take yourself out" (自領出去). Chan thus bends a negative inventory statement into Huineng-linked verse language, an asserted predicate, and a proposition masters can test rather than an imported metaphysical definition.
Senses.Note: The headword and Huineng's longer form are grouped as close morphology but counted separately. The wording "fundamentally, not one teaching" (本無一法) occurs 22 times in 19 texts and remains a related phrase, not an interchangeable occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 自己心原，本無一物，便是成佛。不從萬行漸漸而證
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Collection of the Patriarchal Hall directly predicates the phrase of one's own mind-source and contrasts it with gradual certification.

Occurrences.Kwic: 那畔風光世莫聞，本無一物可呈君。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinyuan Longqi's verse says there is fundamentally not one thing to present.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三頭六臂、千手千眼而本無一物，純真一如、無臭無聲而萬象縱橫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage juxtaposes elaborate bodily forms and myriad appearances with the exact headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 進云：「本無一物，學人參個甚麼？」師云：「自領出去。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student's inference from the phrase becomes a test question and receives a dismissal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩提本無樹。明鏡亦非臺。本來無一物。何處惹塵埃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps transmits Huineng's four-line verse containing the longer close form.

AlternateTargets: complete in itself from the origin
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "from the origin, of itself complete." The phrase occurs 77 times in 53 allowlisted texts. It appears in the Platform Record's list of Huineng's statements on the nature: "who expected the nature to be from the start pure … from the start complete … able to produce the myriad things?" (何期自性本自清淨；何期自性本自具足；何期自性能生萬法). The corpus also turns the wording into a direct question: "what is complete from the start?" The recorded answer is, "because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete" (因無一物可得，所以說具足). A prose criticism asks, "complete from the start—who picks it up or puts it down?" (本自具足，阿誰拈起放下). Other records set the phrase against outside acquisition: living beings are complete from the start and "do not depend on seeking outside" (不假外求). The Zen deployment therefore joins the phrase to the nature, direct questioning, the impossibility of picking it up or putting it down, and explicit refusal of outside acquisition; this entry reports those statements without converting them into a system of cultivation.
Senses.Note: The subjects vary—the nature, unconditioned knowing, living beings, and the matter under discussion—but the predicate remains the same: already complete rather than acquired. These are applications of one predicate, not different things denoted by the phrase itself. The related shorter form "complete" (具足) is broader and may carry ordinary quantitative uses outside this entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何期自性本自清淨何期自性本不生滅何期自性本自具足何期自性本無動搖何期自性能生萬法
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record list attributes to Huineng the statements that the nature is from the start pure, unborn and undying, complete, unmoving, and able to produce the myriad things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：如何是本自具足？王云：因無一物可得，所以說具足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question asks what “complete from the start” is; the answer says that because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本自具足，阿誰拈起放下？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prose criticism asks who could pick up or put down what is complete from the start.

Occurrences.Kwic: 況神通變化眾生本自具足不假外求如今人多是外求
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage says living beings are complete from the start and do not depend on outside seeking, then contrasts this with people who seek outside.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the myriad things return to one
AlternateTargets: the ten thousand things return to one
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the myriad things return to one' (萬法歸一). It most often forms the first clause of the stock question, 'The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一一歸何處). The Zhaozhou case records the answer, 'When I was in Qingzhou I made a cloth shirt weighing seven catties' (我在青州作一領布衫重七斤). The corpus also records other answers under other masters: Wenshu Yingzhen answers, 'The Yellow River has nine bends' (黃河九曲); Luohan Guichen answers, 'There has not been a single person who did not ask' (未有一箇人不問); and later dialogues divide the stock question into 'What is the myriad things returning to one?' (如何是萬法歸一) followed by 'Where does the one finally return?' (畢竟一歸何處). The phrase occurs as the question itself, as the name of the Zhaozhou exchange, in headings for verses on that exchange, and in later masters' renewed questions and answers.
Senses.Note: The exact four-character string occurs 852 times in 219 allowlisted texts. The unpunctuated full question 'the myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一一歸何處) occurs 41 times in 16 texts, while 'where does the one return?' (一歸何處) occurs 755 times in 203 texts. Searches for definition patterns including 'as for the myriad things returning to one' (萬法歸一者), 'the so-called myriad things return to one' (所謂萬法歸一), 'it is called the myriad things return to one' (謂之萬法歸一 and 名為萬法歸一), and 'what is meant by the myriad things returning to one?' (何謂萬法歸一) yielded no direct self-definition. The answers remain attached to their respective speakers; this entry does not turn any one answer into a general gloss for the phrase.
